description:
Hi! We are Team Lux Aeterna, and this is our CLPS Lunar Mission Browser.

The CLPS program is sending commercial landers to the Moon,

where sunlight, Earth line-of-sight and terrain decide whether a mission

survives. We built this tool to make that choice visible: explore multiple

candidate landing sites in 3D, watch the sun and Earth move over time, and

compare sites side by side.

Lux Aeterna means "eternal light," which is what every south-pole lander

is chasing.
summary: Project Lux Aeterna is an interactive, cinematic 3D dashboard designed to help mission planners, educators, and the public visualize the extreme constraints of the lunar South Pole. Using real NASA datasets—including JPL DE421 ephemeris, LRO LOLA altimetry, Diviner thermal maps, and SLDEM2015 slope data—our Python backend calculates 30 days of hourly telemetry for 14 global landing sites. The React and Three.js frontend renders this as a navigable 3D surface with real-time solar tracking, communication blackouts, and battery drain physics. To fulfill the challenge's educational requirement, we built a one-click "Educator Mode" that translates complex aerospace metrics (e.g., 230 Kelvin, 25-degree slope) into plain English ("FREEZING", "TOO STEEP"). The project democratizes complex lunar mission planning by replacing fragmented, multi-gigabyte CLI tools with a unified, accessible web application.
details:
What it does:
The CLPS Lunar Mission Browser is a 3D mission planning engine. It visualizes the complex lighting and communication constraints of the lunar South Pole. Users can select from 14 historic and future landing sites, scrub through a 30-day mission timeline, and watch as the 3D terrain shadows shift, the lander's battery drains, and the communication link to Earth drops in and out.

How it works:

  1. Data Pipeline: We used Python, Skyfield, and Rasterio to parse raw NASA GeoTIFFs and JPL ephemeris data into lightweight JSON files. We simulated lander physics (solar generation vs. 50W system drain) to calculate battery levels.
  2. Frontend: Built with React, Three.js (React Three Fiber), and Tailwind CSS. The 3D terrain is generated dynamically from NASA heightmaps.

Benefits & Impact:
Mission planners currently have to cross-reference massive, raw datasets in specialized software. Our tool provides instant, visual, actionable intelligence. Furthermore, the "Educator Mode" makes it perfect for classrooms, directly addressing NASA's goal of inspiring the Artemis Generation.

Tools & Creative Factors:
We considered the extreme thermal and terrain hazards of the South Pole. The app features a "Water Ice (ISRU)" metric derived from the Lemelin et al. 2021 dataset, showing users exactly where future astronauts could harvest fuel and drinking water. We pushed the boundaries of web-based 3D rendering to make the terrain feel cinematic and immersive.
projectRefs: Lemelin et al. 2021 PSR Water Ice Database
